analysis.one_liner: Ends the special exemption letting oil and gas drilling waste escape hazardous-waste disposal rules.
analysis.headline: The bill would have closed a decades-old exemption that lets oil and gas drilling waste escape hazardous-waste rules, but it never received a hearing or vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal hazardous-waste law has long contained a special exemption: waste from drilling for oil, natural gas, or geothermal energy — drilling fluids, produced waters, and similar byproducts — does not have to be regulated as hazardous waste, no matter what is in it. The CLEANER Act would have removed that loophole. Within a year of passage, the EPA would have to decide whether this drilling waste meets the hazardous-waste criteria, write disposal rules for whatever qualifies, and tighten the rules for landfills that accept the rest — including ground-water monitoring to catch contamination, standards for where facilities can be located, cleanup requirements, and proof of funds to pay for them. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee in March 2021 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near oil and gas wells, drilling-waste pits, and the landfills or injection sites that take drilling waste — who currently have no federal hazardous-waste protection from that waste. Ground-water monitoring, siting standards, cleanup requirements, and financial assurance would make contamination easier to detect and pay for. Communities near the roughly 1.7 million oil and gas wells and thousands of disposal wells in the United States would see the strongest protections; drinking-water supplies would be the clearest winner.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living near drilling waste sites

how_it_helps.text: It ends the special exemption that has kept oil and gas drilling waste outside the nation's hazardous-waste rules since the 1980s, requiring the EPA to determine whether that waste is hazardous.

If the EPA finds the waste hazardous, it must write disposal regulations, with the flexibility to adapt the rules to the special characteristics of drilling waste so long as human health and the environment are protected [S3].

Even for waste that stays nonhazardous, the bill requires tighter rules for landfills and disposal facilities that take it — including ground-water monitoring to detect contamination, siting criteria, corrective action, and financial assurance so cleanup money exists when something goes wrong.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, who would bear the cost of characterizing their waste and sending it to permitted facilities — hazardous disposal costs more than the ordinary landfill or pit disposal the exemption currently allows. Geothermal operators are covered by the same provisions. Those costs could reach consumers through energy prices, and some waste currently going to ordinary landfills would have to shift to more expensive permitted facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and drillers

drawbacks.text: Regulating drilling waste as hazardous would raise disposal costs for oil and gas producers, costs that could be passed on to consumers through higher energy prices and could fall hardest on smaller operators.

The bill gives the EPA only one year to study the waste, make a hazardous determination, and write new disposal rules — an aggressive timeline that, if rushed, could produce poorly designed regulations for both hazardous and nonhazardous drilling waste.

Supporters of the existing exemption have long argued that drilling fluids and produced waters are generated in enormous volumes and mostly resemble ordinary industrial waste, so full hazardous-waste regulation could overwhelm permitted disposal facilities; the bill tries to address this by allowing the EPA to tailor requirements to the special characteristics of drilling waste [S3], but the volume concern remains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: closing a decades-old loophole would subject oil and gas drilling waste to the same hazardous-waste scrutiny as other toxic waste, with ground-water monitoring and cleanup requirements that protect people living near wells and disposal sites [S2][S3]. The cost, which an honest supporter would acknowledge, is that tightening disposal rules would raise waste-handling costs for drillers — costs that could be passed to consumers or, in a weak market, discourage some marginal drilling — and it would impose a one-year regulatory sprint on the EPA [S2][S3]. On balance, the public-health and water-protection gains outweigh the disposal-cost increases, particularly given the bill's flexibility to tailor requirements to the special characteristics of drilling waste [S3]. The larger design question is moot, however, because the bill never advanced past its first committee referral [S1][S5].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its environment subcommittee, where no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened, and it expired when the term ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced H.R. 2132 on March 23, 2021, with 39 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change the next day [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never reported the bill, the House never debated it, and the Senate never considered it [S1][S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers come out ahead, since they keep disposing of drilling fluids and produced waters under the looser solid-waste rules rather than hazardous-waste standards. Landfills and disposal facilities handling drilling waste also avoid new monitoring and cleanup requirements.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Oil and natural gas producers and trade groups
against.what_they_did: Long-standing, well-documented opposition to revoking the regulatory exemption for drilling waste, the exemption this bill would have eliminated.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 initial supporters, including the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor joined, and with Democrats holding only a narrow House majority, the bill had no path past a committee controlled by its own party.

industries.note: Producers currently dispose of drilling fluids and produced waters under the looser solid-waste rules; classifying this waste as hazardous would raise their waste-handling and disposal costs [S2][S3]. Those costs are the reason the exemption exists. Ordinary people near well sites bear the contamination risk the bill would address.

If drilling waste is reclassified as hazardous, it must be handled by permitted hazardous-waste facilities, creating new demand for that industry [S2][S3]. Its interest runs alongside the public's here: the same rules that send it business are the ones protecting water.

The bill requires revised criteria — ground-water monitoring, siting standards, corrective action, and financial assurance — for landfills and other facilities that receive nonhazardous drilling waste, imposing compliance costs [S3].
